evidence: Quint. 9.4.61: neque enim loquī possumus nisi syllabīs brevibus ac longīs
Cic. Par. 26: syllaba brevior aut longior (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Letters make syllables and syllables make words: litterae faciunt syllabās, syllabae faciunt dictiōnēs (Traupman 247, 249). On which syllable the stress falls: In quā syllabā accentum pōnimus? (Traupman 237).

phrases.latin: neque enim loquī possumus nisi syllabīs brevibus ac longīs, ex quibus pedēs fīunt
phrases.english: for we cannot speak except in short and long syllables, from which feet are made

sources: John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 237, 247, 249.
Quintilian checked against the Perseus Latin texts, and cited by its numbering.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
